steps.title: Match bank to ledger lines exactly (pandas)
steps.what: A pandas script, written with Claude Code, pairs lines with the same date and amount one-to-one: 167 of 197 bank lines matched.
steps.code:
b = bank.assign(k=bank.groupby(["date", "amount"]).cumcount())
g = ledger.assign(k=ledger.groupby(["date", "amount"]).cumcount())
exact = b.merge(g, on=["date", "amount", "k"], suffixes=("_bank", "_gl"))

steps.title: Add rules for near matches: dates, amounts, payee names
steps.what: Rules catch ACH lines that clear a few days late and card charges a few cents off, using difflib to match payee names: 24 more matched, 6 bank + 3 ledger lines left over.
steps.code:
cands = cands[(cands.days <= 5) & (cands["diff"].abs() <= 1.0)]
cands["name"] = [name_score(d, p) for d, p in zip(cands.description, cands.payee)]
cands = cands[cands.name >= 0.45]   # SequenceMatcher ratio / word overlap

story.situation: A 60-person company closes its books in about 6 working days. Two of those days go to ticking bank lines against the ledger in spreadsheets, and odd items are found late.
story.constraints: The numbers must be exact and auditable, so matching is plain pandas code, never a model. Bank and ledger data stay inside the finance tenant. The controller approves every journal entry; nothing posts automatically.
story.replay: Reuse: 'rules do the bulk, the model explains the leftovers' fits any matching job (invoices to POs, payouts to orders, claims to remits). Next time: feed the controller's decisions back as new rules, so the leftover pile shrinks every month.
